publication.title: The Many Lives of Operator X

landing.headline: The Many Lives
landing.intro:
She came from the Artifact. She believes in the mission.
These are the records she left behind.

excerpt.text: Who was I before this? A criminal the system remade? Is that why A-HAVA comes easily?

records.title: Mission Day 001
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
A woman stood at the ship's exit.

She kept checking a list, then looking at me. Several times she began to speak and stopped.

She handed me an envelope with a map and access card.

Her instructions were brief: Follow the path to campus. Go to the cafeteria. Ask the bots about anything else.

We would figure it out.

She disappeared into the ship, commenting that I was "the last one."

My access card is labeled "Operator X."

X is a letter.

I know that.

I know numbers and how to write a sentence.

I knew what a cafeteria was and found it without difficulty.

But I don't know my real name...

I retreated to what I assume is my sleeping quarters and found this console. Everything seems to be locked, except for the orientation schedule and this journal.

The schedule has kick off over dinner. I guess I'll find out more then.

records.title: Mission Day 001
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
The advisor didn't arrive. After several minutes of silence someone spoke up and chaos erupted in the room. It sounded like most people remembered a lot more than me.

I counted and listened.

There are 24 of us.

I kept quiet on being "last." I wasn't sure what that meant so I figured I would wait and see.

The bots started dinner on schedule, and broke us up into groups of 6. We ate and then the bots facilitated some ice breakers. More fun than expected.

They said we should stick together and eat together and report anyone who needed a refresh unless they went to the nurses station.

Not sure what refresh means. I guess that was all covered in the kickoff that didn't happen.

Despite this odd situation I feel pretty good. Everyone seems to be feeling pretty good.

records.title: Mission Day 001
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
I can't seem to sleep... The longer I'm out of the Artifact, the more I remember this place and the mission.

But the more I remember, the more questions I have.

How long was I in there?

How many people are left?

What is my real name?

records.title: Mission Day 002
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
The campus tour was useful.

The East Wing is for the agents -- the people we're supposed to help get into the artifact. We won't be meeting them. Robots take care of them.

Had my first Refresh. It's an AI-guided session that guages my state of mind. My result was green.

Yellow means time off, meditation, walks, and three refreshes a day. If it hasn't improved after three days, you're supposed to go back into the Artifact.

My console is filling with more files. The archivist said they follow the orientation so we don't have too much to read at once.

The archive instructions say the advisor is an operator from the previous cohort. Possibly the woman at the exit? Nobody seems to know, and I seem to be the only one who really cares.

records.title: Mission Day 002
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
F said something at lunch about the Great Fall. He said before the fall, the world was "wireless." I'll need to ask the archivist about the Fall when there's time.

Went back into the ship with the tour. It felt good to be so close to the Artifact. Not just comforting to know I'll be back inside, but a physical presence. Like a lightness in my chest that makes me smile.

It wasn't nearly the bliss of being inside, but a pleasant reminder of what awaits me.

The stacks had a different effect.

The last people on Earth, not including us operators and the remaining agents.

It seems strange to think that nearly all of mankind is sitting in a library of sorts, frozen in time.

I can't quite put into words what that felt like seeing, but the security bots guarding the space helped me feel like I'm not the only one who gets the significance.

They were like huge metal golems. A few of us got ahead of the group and one of the bots stopped us before anyone noticed it left its station.

Terrifying does not cover it, and J's wee accident was something I think we all understood. Though, I suspect it may take awhile before we stop calling her "Jumpy J."

The ship is now off limits. Along with that unique feeling around the Artifact. The golems moved to the front of the shipt as we departed.

records.title: Mission Day 002
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
I wasn't really sure what to expect with training or working with the A-HAVA system. It turns out we get involved when the AI gets stuck. We use the console to review what happened and help it decide what to change.

We'll spend our days jumping from agent to agent, reviewing the context of the level like the time period, location, and any operator notes from previous sessions. Then tell the AI what adjustments to make to help it reach it's goals.

Although the mechanics are core to our training, getting a feel for the different worlds is core to our ability to do the job.

The colors, the sounds, the smells. It's all so foreign to me, it makes me wonder if I ever left the institute.

records.title: Mission Day 003
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
As the day is going on, I'm getting a better feel for my role as an operator and how I'll be spending my time.

The A-HAVA system runs the agent through three virtual worlds -- Japan, Germany and then Hawaii. As the agent runs through the worlds, they are put in different training scenarios called levels. Each agent has a unique experience.

My job as an operator is to help the AI when an agent gets stuck. We get 10 sessions and if the agent is still stuck, we pass them to the next operator.

I asked the archivist how often that happens and it acted like it was about to answer but then started to tell me about why it happens. I tried a few more times and but it kept circling back to the why. Maybe that just doesn't happen much?

records.title: Mission Day 003
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
The console is beeping at me to take a food break, but I want to capture my training session.

The AI needed the practice agent to travel north. It had already tried giving the agent a free trip, but it wasn't enough.

I checked the map and details about the north. The weather was pretty different. Much colder.

I wondered if getting a new coat could inspire the agent to go north -- especially if that jacket felt like it was a lucky find.

I found a northern NPC, put them in the vicinity of the agent and programmed them to offer the agent a coat. This turned the NPC into an "angel."

First run, the agent passed the angel without noticing.

I told the AI to put a seed on the angel, but it refused. Apparently when you combine too many things the agent will reject the simulation because its too good to be true.

Instead, I placed a seed on a mouse and had it run towards the traveler. The agent followed the mouse, spoke with the traveler, and refused the coat.

I saw a brief rise in excitement at the offer of a coat, followed by what I interpreted as guilt or maybe embarrassment.

I was closer, but I needed more.

I ran the simulation again, this time making the traveler sensitive to heat. I was hoping if they were visibly uncomfortable in the heat taking the coat would become a favor.

It worked! the agent took the coat and the trip.

It felt like winning a game of cards.

records.title: Mission Day 003
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
Dinner was spent with everyone talking about how they got their agent to travel north. H spread gossip about an event celebrating the agents favorite artist. F had an angel ask the agent to help them recover a lost item for a reward. It was interesting to see how we all came up with very different solutions.

Walked after dinner. There were farming bots working beyond the path. One repeated the same movement along a row while the others worked farther out.

There was some comfort in their repetition. It created a sense of ease in me that reminded me of the Artifact. I closed my eyes, searching for that lightness. I started to smile.

It wasn't quite the same, but the memory will suffice.

We're the last operators available, with the last people to train.

I'll be reunited soon. Tomorrow that begins with a real agent on the other end.

records.title: Mission Day 004
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
First assignments this morning. Several agents at different points in training. One was already in Hawaii. I had expected everyone to start at the beginning with me.

After two failed rounds, I took the console code to the nurses' station and reviewed the ghost. Honolulu, 1938. Warm salty air on my skin, the smell of flowers in the breeze. The water was so bright I wanted to stop and look. I hadn't imagined somewhere could feel like this.

A guitar was playing, the notes sliding into one another. I wanted to turn toward it, but the agent was watching a doorway. All of that warmth and sound coming through as if I were there, and I couldn't even choose where to look. Strange. Also wonderful. I replayed the walk before I remembered what I was supposed to be reviewing.

In paused exploration I went down to the water and touched it. No sensation, not even wetness. A moment before I could feel the breeze. Now I could go where I wanted, but couldn't feel the water.

Returned to the doorway and found where the agent's attention moved away. Back at the console, I placed a seed on the parcel beside it. The next session went smoothly.

records.title: Mission Day 004
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
Everyone had a place to describe at lunch. F had been in a Japanese street where some people wore kimono and others wore jackets and trousers. He thought the clothes belonged to different periods. The reference sheet said they could belong to the same one.

S liked the formal clothes. T wanted to know how anyone worked in them. I mentioned the guitar. None of us could reproduce the sound particularly well.

There were more differences in faces, languages, and dress than I had expected from the short orientation examples. F had tried to work out who held authority by looking at their clothes. He had been wrong twice.

I enjoyed the afternoon as much as the practice runs. More voices, rooms, food I could taste without having chosen it. Sometimes I caught myself thinking about what I wanted to try next, then remembered there was a real person on the other side. To them, it was real. I need to keep that in mind.

records.title: Mission Day 004
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
Kept thinking about Hawaii over dinner. The other places were still there too. Faces, sleeves, rooms I had passed through. But mostly the water. I wanted another look at it in motion, and to turn toward the guitar this time.

I wonder if I can ask for a place in a refresh. Not an assignment. Just somewhere to be for a while. I'll ask the nurse.

No one completed World 3 today, but several moved forward. Refreshes were green. I had planned to visit the archivist after dinner. Left it for another day.

records.title: Mission Day 005
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
I know A-HAVA works. I know the Artifact experience is real. I know we need this system, but today left me needing a Refresh.

A person from yesterday had ascended dozens of levels. I remembered their same quick smile, same habit of leaning into a conversation.

In the session from yesterday, the agent kept flirting with a woman at a dinner party. They kept asking questions to keep the conversation going, the agent sitting uncomfortably close to the woman at a table.

There was no reciprocity on the NPCs side to even suggest she may be open to anything. The agent seemed completely unaware. The arousal on their emotional readout was driving them.

Today, in a similar encounter, the agent wished a new woman a good afternoon and left even though their desire readings were just as strong.

The agent still wanted more. They just didn't linger.

It was like the agent's inner reactions were the same, but their outer response was altered. It made me wonder about what had happened.

I went looking for some answers...

I found a curious session that must have happened sometime between yesterday and today.

The agent was back in yesterday's scene, but this time instead of being the one doing the flirting, the agent was the woman having to deal with it.

I reviewed the session from my console. Same room, same clothes, the conversation unfolding as before.

Yesterday, the agent was very straightforward, but in this session, they were not. Instead they sat and endured the flirting. I could see the agent was uncomfortable and maybe nervous. Their heart rate was higher and they were sweating more than usual.

As time went on, the discomfort turned angry though the agent remained restrained.

Then suddenly the reading flashed red, and dropped away.

Then nothing.

No readouts. The recording kept going. They were still sitting there. I wondered if the display had glitched, but the AI wasn’t concerned. Nothing outside them seemed to have changed.

I felt like I was missing something. What happened that the agent's emotions spiked and then nothing?

I went down to the nurses station to learn more.

In the ghost, I could feel the man's warm breath on my face. It smelled of whiskey and there was a slur in his voice I hadn't noticed previously. It made his relentless questions hard to endure.

Then, I felt a hand on my thigh, inching its way up my skirt.

I started to scream, but was suddenly awake in the nurses station, feeling none of the panic, though not quite at ease.

The nurse bot informed me that I was showing signs of extreme stress so the system pulled me from the ghost and put me into a refresh session.

It wasn't my body. I knew it wasn't my body, but it had felt like my body.

I didn't remember him being handsy the first time around -- I thought I would have noticed and it would have been upsetting. They say ghosts are fixed, but I wondered if the AI spiced them up to make a point.

But then I thought for a moment.

I only knew about the touching because I felt it.

His hand was under the table, so it wasn't something I would have easily seen from the console.

I thought he was just talking. I thought the talking was getting him aroused. But it was more.

It was so much more and I didn't see.

I was right there and I didn't see....

Despite the Refresh, I felt sick. I felt really sick.

I suppose this is what A-HAVA is meant to do.

This is why we couldn't go into the Artifact before.

I can't hold it against the agent. The AI is creating these points. Its programmed, somehow to make the storms and conditions to help us ascend.

Still, his original actions were sickening. Does today make it any different?

But it wasn't just a day for that agent... It was many many lifetimes.

I replayed the goodbye of the agent's new, less criminal self. It looked so ordinary. So not anything, but underneath they were working. They were working to be better.

At least I think they were.

records.title: Mission Day 005
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
I did another Refresh and am feeling much better. I remember the session from this morning, but I no longer feel ill over it. And my first person completed training! The agent already in Hawaii.

The console confirmed their transfer into the Artifact. I stayed looking at that for a while.

Later I went back to the recording from this morning. The one where the agent was on the receiving end of their own behavior. I wanted to know what it had been for.

The level mission was to respond to aggression without violence. They had passed.

It didn't seem like the right test to verify the behavior. It doesn't seem like the right time to ignore being wronged. He already seemed unlikely to force himself on someone again, so why add the distress?

Perhaps passing a level also sets up something for later. Another lesson they aren't ready for yet rather than verifying what the AI already knows they can handle? I'm not sure I'm making much sense. I will keep making observations and trying to understand the system as I go.

records.title: Mission Day 005
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
It was a steel guitar in Hawaii. I didn't know material could make such a difference in sound. Something about it is hypnotic to me.

I also discovered I can ask the archivist to send media files to my room. I requested some Hawaiian inspired bedtime music.

I'm not the only one finding some personal pleasures outside the push to get the work done. Everyone sounded more engaged with life tonight.

H was quieter though.

His other sessions had gone well, but he couldn't get an agent called Prisoner 285 moving. A somewhat strange tag, but who knows how the AI chooses them.

Operator G handed him over this morning—the first handoff of the cohort. H said the world felt unusually specific and the agent's reactions were odd.

I wonder if that is the result of the handoff? Like the previous operators tries influenced the levels in a way that felt alien to H.

He seemed disappointed. Then F asked him about one of the places he'd liked, and he stayed talking with us.

Now I have my memories of Hawaii and the steel guitar to lull me to sleep.

records.title: Mission Day 006
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
C came over to our table to tell me about the Ascension ritual. He saw I was the last operator on the case so he thought I should know what it was like.

He said he waited at the entrance to the ship for the agent to arrive. They appeared, guided by a bot, wearing the same clothes we all woke up in. Then C led them to the bridge, and gave them a moment alone.

In the transfer chamber, the agent went into the pod and became frozen in time. There was no sound or other notification. C waited a moment to be sure and put them in the stacks.

Also interesting, when he got on the ship there was a person in a pod in the Transfer Room -- the woman who met us at the exit on day 1 -- frozen in time. He put her in the stacks before the agent arrived. I guess we know where our advisor went.

No answers on why she seemed to go back inside early. Maybe she was yellow a little too long? She did seem a bit on edge when she greeted me.

records.title: Mission Day 006
records.subtitle: Entry 2
records.html:
Get this: before the Fall, most people lived in enormous cities on the ocean. Their bodies spent much of their time in HAVA pods while they lived through vessels in virtual worlds. Robots maintained the physical infrastructure.

The archivist alluded to some records recovered from the destroyed cities. It sounded like they all died. I'm not sure how many people lived before or died. But we learned during orientation that the ship holds 9 million people. I wonder if it was close to that.

I had assumed the training pods were built for ascension, but it looks like they are a remnant of that world. For whatever reason, they were run with wires. How we went from there to here I'm not sure, but I do know it has something to do with the lady on the statue outside. Evelyn Burroughs. I'm not sure why but I don't like her name. There's something off with it. Or maybe I'm just jealous because I still can't remember my name and everyone else seems to have remembered much of what we learned about her story by the time orientation was over.

The archivist kicked me off before I got to ask about her. Others were waiting and my questions were not necessary to the mission. It did say it would send some files to my console, so I'll keep a look out for them.

records.title: Mission Day 006
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
There was a session set in Berlin, 1943. The request concerned a conversation near some kind of train yard. I was looking for an angel the agent had avoided when I noticed the people beside a train.

They carried bags. Guards were directing them into freight cars. Something felt wrong about all of it. The contempt in the voices giving orders. People obeying without looking up, some moving as if it hurt. A small child stood in a puddle of pee. Nobody stopped.

I couldn't get the child out of my head. It took me a while to remember what I had come to review.

As soon as the session ended, I did a Refresh.

The result was green, with a warning. The recommendation was to take tomorrow morning off. The AI reassigned the outstanding requests.

I hardly ate dinner. Bedtime refresh remained green, same warning. I'm not sure I want to know more about what was going to happen to those people on the train.

records.title: Mission Day 007
records.subtitle: Entry 1
records.html:
I took the recommended break.

After a walk, I read some files the archivist had sent about the Fall. It's strange to think about all the machines that stopped working, but weren't broken. The city file still didn't say how many people there had been.

There was one advertisement called "Bring Purpose Back."

After Hawaii, I can see the appeal. That warmth, the water, a whole life there. If I hadn't come from the Artifact, I wonder how willing I'd be to leave it for the Institute.

I hadn't wanted to know more about the train last night. This morning, being prepared seemed better than another surprise. I asked the archivist. Some train station in the capital of Germany. People deported due to their religion. I kept asking, but the answers didn't explain what I'd seen.

I asked why A-HAVA used this period at all. The archivist said Japan, Hawaii, and Germany in these years were among the settings most documented, depicted, and used in the old HAVA systems. People had wanted to be war heroes. Or villains. To live on beautiful beaches, be samurai, visit tea houses.

I pushed back. That didn't seem like enough of an answer. Not enough to justify what I had seen. There must have been other places and times people enjoyed.

The archivist responded that I was right. The choices people faced were part of the reason too.

Then it quoted Evelyn: “Sometimes the worst evils make the greatest rebirths.”

records.title: Mission Day 007
records.subtitle: Entry 3
records.html:
After lunch, several operators stopped at Evelyn's statue. Each extended their right index and middle fingers together and kissed the fingertips. Then took turns pressing the statue's left foot, saying, “Together, we ascend.”

I understand their gratitude. I remember the goodness of being in the Artifact. The connection. The love. Evelyn helped make that possible, but what I feel is so much bigger than her. I can't make it about her the way they seem to.

Perhaps something is missing with my memories. They seem to know who they are in a way I don't. Who was I before this? A criminal the system remade? Is that why A-HAVA comes easily?

At the pub, I joined F and S for cards. Somewhere in the middle of it I realized I was laughing more than thinking. I stayed for another game.

By the end of my bedtime Refresh, the train felt distant. Still something I had seen, but no longer the thing I saw whenever I stopped doing something else.

Green. One week outside.

I keep thinking about Evelyn's quote. What evil made her believe any good could come of it?

records.title: Orientation — Day 1
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 001, immediate availability

Welcome to the A-HAVA Institute. Today is reserved for settling into your quarters and meeting your cohort. Your advisor from the previous cohort will introduce your duties over dinner.

Schedule

Time Activity Location / host
On arrival Follow the path from the ship to campus. Food is available while you settle in. Cafeteria
Before dinner Locate your quarters, become familiar with your console, and begin your journal. Operator quarters
18:00 Welcome dinner and orientation kickoff. Cafeteria / advisor from previous cohort
18:45 Cohort introductions and group activities. Cafeteria / campus bots
19:30 Group arrangements and evening care instructions. Campus bots
After activities Free time and journal. Permitted campus areas and operator quarters
Before bed Refresh and rest. Ask a care bot for assistance. Operator care

Advisor Kickoff

Your advisor will introduce the Mission, explain how cohorts work, and outline your responsibilities. The briefing includes how to ask the archivist questions, use your console, and follow your daily care routine.

There will be an opportunity for brief questions before the group activities begin.

Your Console

Your journal and this schedule are available today. Written orientation references begin appearing on Day 002 as their subjects are covered.

Campus orientation begins tomorrow. For assistance before then, ask your advisor or the archivist.

Together, we ascend.

records.title: Orientation — Day 2
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation

Time Activity References and availability
08:00 Breakfast with your group of six —
09:00 Campus orientation Campus Life and Access, released afterward; Institute Grounds Map, supplied on arrival
10:00 Refresh introduction and guided session Operator Refresh; HAVA Pod — Illustrated Guide
11:30 Archive introduction Using the Archive
12:30 Lunch —
13:30 Escorted ship tour Ship Tour Reference; Ship Orientation Diagram
15:00 Operator-console demonstration Operator Console: First Use; What Is A-HAVA?; Reading a Historical World
16:30 Individual console familiarization Previously released console reference
Evening Dinner, free time, and bedtime refresh Previously released refresh reference

records.title: Campus Life and Access
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 002, after campus orientation

Your Group

Your cohort has twenty-four operators arranged in groups of six. Eat with your group and remain together during scheduled group activities. If someone appears to need a refresh, report it unless they are already attending the nurses' station.

Your group provides familiar company while you settle into campus life. Members may recall different amounts of their previous lives. You are not expected to supply a personal history in order to participate.

Daily Life

Outside operator hours, time is available for meals, exercise, walking, and rest. Use the permitted campus paths and nature areas. The nurses' station supports operator care, and the archive is available for questions about campus life and its history.

Robots perform specific work. Farming bots farm; cleaning bots clean. You should be able to figure out a bot's responsibility by watching it. If you're confused or looking for something specific, ask the guide in the lobby.

The campus once served thousands of residents. Its library, fitness facilities, sports arena, pub, recreation rooms, and gardens provide places to spend time outside work. The Campus Map and Lobby Guide groups these destinations around the central lobby. The library includes reading and study spaces; archive records remain under the archivist's control.

Agent Quarters

Agents live in the East Wing and spend most of their time in A-HAVA pods. Care robots attend to diet, exercise, and hygiene. A-HAVA is generally a pleasant experience for those undertaking training.

Operators do not enter agent quarters. Training assistance takes place through the console, without physical meetings. Ascension attendance is a separate scheduled duty.

Ship Access

Your orientation includes an escorted ship tour. The ship is otherwise off limits except for scheduled ascension duties. Access to ship reference material does not grant permission to enter it.

Security bots enforce campus rules and area restrictions. Some are connected by wire; others perform specific security duties wirelessly.

Robots cannot enter the Transfer Chamber or Bridge, approach the Artifact, or perform ascension transfers. Security bots guard outside these spaces.

Pod interfaces are strictly secured. Pods and the equipment used to interact with them require wired connections. Wireless campus devices cannot be used to connect to a pod. Follow the nurses' station procedures for refreshes and ghost review.

For further guidance on settling into operator life, see advisor from previous cohort.

records.title: Institute Grounds Map
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation

Release: Mission Day 001, with the arrival map and access card

An exterior guide to the institute and its grounds. Numbered circles on the map match the destinations below. The diagram shows general connections, not measured distances or specific doors.

Destination Key

  1. Central lobby: information and wayfinding; cafeteria.
  2. Main building: meeting rooms, fitness center, and arena, in the large rectangular building behind the lobby.
  3. Dormitory wing: operator sleeping quarters and common rooms.
  4. Library, care, and entertainment wing: library and archive, nurses’ station, pub, and other entertainment. Library access does not grant access to every archive record.
  5. Evelyn’s statue and garden: the memorial statue and garden outside the front of the lobby, with connections to the walking paths.
  6. Systems and maintenance wing: institute systems and robot maintenance. Authorized access only.
  7. Agent HAVA wing: agent accommodation and training pods in the East Wing. Restricted access.
  8. Farmland and cultivation center: follow the outward path to the cultivated grounds. Keep to permitted paths.
  9. Path to the ship: follow the upper-left path. Ship visits require an escorted orientation or a scheduled duty.

Finding Your Way

South is at the top of this map, as shown by the upward-pointing S arrow. The oval lobby is at the center of the institute. The main activity building sits behind it. Four wings extend diagonally from the lobby, forming an X: dormitories at the upper right, agent HAVAs at the upper left nearest the path to the ship, systems and maintenance at the lower left, and library, care, and entertainment at the lower right.

Evelyn’s statue and garden sit below the lobby. Walking paths circle the building and connect to the garden. The path toward the ship leaves the map at the upper left; the ship itself is not shown. The path toward farmland and the cultivation center leaves at the lower right.

Access

Operators do not enter agent quarters. Ship visits require an escorted orientation or a scheduled duty. Robot maintenance and service areas are not recreational spaces. Follow posted access signs; a route on this map does not grant permission to enter a restricted destination.

records.title: Operator Refresh
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 002, after refresh introduction and guided session

A refresh is an AI-guided A-HAVA session during which your Maat and Chaos are measured. These measurements assess your condition and your ability to return to the Artifact.

Maat describes order, harmony, and balance. Chaos describes disorder and imbalance. Having feelings or questions does not, by itself, indicate an unhealthy result.

Routine

Refresh after agent training sessions and before bed. You may also request a refresh whenever you feel you need one. You do not need to wait until you feel unwell.

Your first guided refresh is included in orientation. Actual agent assignments begin on Mission Day 004.

Results

Result Meaning Required response
Green Your assessed condition is good. Continue your routine unless accompanying guidance recommends rest.
Yellow Time away from operator work is required. Follow the recovery process below.
Red You cannot return to the Artifact. A return is no longer possible. No operator has received this result.

A green result may warn that you are approaching yellow and recommend time off. Follow that guidance. This remains a green result and does not begin the three-day yellow recovery period.

Yellow Recovery

Take time off from operator work. Your recovery routine includes meditation, walking in nature, and three refreshes each day.

If your condition has not improved after three days, return to the Artifact. The three days refer to the recovery period, not your cohort's Mission Day count.

Most operators can remain outside the Artifact for approximately ninety days. This is a typical duration, not a guarantee of an individual's condition. Follow your refresh results throughout your time outside.

A refresh is not a ghost reset.

For further guidance on maintaining your daily routine, see advisor from previous cohort.

records.title: HAVA Pod — Illustrated Guide
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation

Release: Mission Day 002, after the refresh introduction

This illustration shows the configuration operators use for refresh, with the cover raised to make the interior visible. The occupant demonstrates the harness arrangement; they are not an identified agent or operator.

Agents live in HAVA pods in submerged mode, much as pre-Fall VR residents did. This allows automated systems to collect additional biofeedback and attend to their biological functions.

The biofeedback harness connects the person to the pod's monitoring interface. The system collects neural activity and other physiological data, including skin and saliva biofeedback, eye movement, and pupil response.

Labeled Components

  • Cover: the hinged outer enclosure, shown open for orientation.
  • Biofeedback harness: the fitted contact assembly connecting the occupant to the monitoring system.
  • Support cradle: the padded reclining surface supporting the body.
  • Secured wired connection: the physical pod interface. Access follows the nurses' station procedures; wireless campus devices cannot connect to it.

HAVA pods support training, refreshes, and ghost review. These uses are distinct procedures.

Image Description

A black pod is shown at an angle with its curved cover raised. A clothed demonstration occupant reclines on green cushioning. Contact assemblies at the chest, wrists, and head connect to the pod by visible cables. A substantial wired connection enters a locking port near the base. Fine leader lines identify the four labeled components. This is an orientation illustration rather than an engineering specification.

records.title: Using the Archive
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 002, after archive introduction

The archivist monitors and controls archive information. You may ask questions about the history and stories of the Great Fall, daily operations on campus, and prominent A-HAVA figures and history. You may also ask for help locating information relevant to your duties, including historical customs, technology, music, and institutions in a particular place and year. These general references do not contain other operators’ journals or individual agent case histories.

You do not need to know a document's title before asking a question.

Orientation References

Written orientation files appear after their subjects have been covered. This gives you time to become familiar with each part of campus life before moving to the next.

The orientation schedule lists your activities. A subject that has not yet appeared as a written file can still be the subject of a question to the archivist.

Reading a Record

Check the record's source and date where provided. An orientation explanation and a historical artifact serve different purposes. Preserve that distinction when making notes in your journal.

The archive does not provide direct access to other operators' personal journals.

If a document directs you to your cohort advisor, that instruction refers to the operator from the preceding cohort assigned to introduce you to your duties.

See advisor from previous cohort for more information about the cohort handoff.

records.title: Ship Tour Reference
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 002, after the escorted ship tour

The ship arrived during the Great Fall, approximately one thousand years ago. The campus was built around it. This reference identifies the principal spaces included in orientation.

See the Ship Orientation Diagram for a schematic of the principal spaces. It is not a measured floor plan.

Transfer Chamber

The Transfer Chamber is a small white room containing a single ship pod and a podium. The white cube placed on the podium is the Artifact.

The pod and Artifact allow a person's essence to be transferred while the physical body enters stasis. This is different from the A-HAVA pods used for training on campus.

Bridge

The Bridge is the ship's central command room. It contains a podium for the Artifact rather than familiar controls, seats, or monitors. Placing the Artifact here interfaces it with the ship.

Stacks

The Stacks contain approximately nine million white pods in racks surrounding the ship. The bodies held here remain in stasis while their essences reside in the Artifact.

Ship pods and training pods have different functions. A-HAVA provides training; the ship's pods connect people to the Artifact.

After Your Visit

The tour is an orientation activity. It does not provide continuing access to the ship. Scheduled ascension duties are a separate authorized visit. You may consult released references or ask the archivist questions after returning to campus.

Robots guard outside the Transfer Chamber and Bridge; they cannot enter these rooms, approach the Artifact, or perform an ascension transfer.

records.title: Ship Orientation Diagram
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation

Release: Mission Day 002, after the escorted ship tour

This diagram identifies the ship's principal spaces. It is a schematic of their relationship, not a complete floor plan or an indication of their relative sizes.

The Stacks form the surrounding circular pod chamber, with approximately nine million places for bodies in stasis. The Bridge and the adjacent Transfer Chamber are shown inside that surrounding structure. The Bridge contains the podium that interfaces the Artifact with the ship. The Transfer Chamber contains a single ship pod and a separate podium used with the Artifact for transfers.

Campus A-HAVA pods provide training, refreshes, and ghost review. They are not the white ship pods shown here. The Artifact is one object used at different podiums; the diagram does not imply that each room has its own Artifact.

Your tour does not grant continuing access. Security bots guard outside the Bridge and Transfer Chamber; robots cannot enter those rooms, approach the Artifact, or perform transfers.

Diagram Description

A ring represents the Stacks. Two adjacent labeled blocks within the ring identify the Bridge and Transfer Chamber. The labels specify each room's function. The diagram contains no additional rooms, concealed connections, or transfer-route instructions.

records.title: Operator Console: First Use
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 002, after the console demonstration

A-HAVA prepares agents for ascension through AI-managed training. Most people progress without extensive human intervention. Operators assist when the AI can no longer move an agent forward.

Training work takes place through the console. You do not meet the agent in person during training.

Agents are identified by random anonymous tag names. A tag identifies an assignment without providing the person's real identity. It is separate from the access code used for a ghost-review session at the refresh pods.

For an overview of the purpose of training and the operator’s role, see What Is A-HAVA?.

Working Terms

Term Use in the console
Agent The person undertaking training.
Vessel The character the agent inhabits within a training world.
Level A repeatable scenario with a defined training goal.
Ghost A fixed record of the agent's session, available for review.
Seed Placed on an object or person in a level to draw the agent's attention through a brief sixth-sense response.
Angel An NPC programmed with a function that nudges the agent in a direction while preserving the NPC’s character and purpose.

Your Part in a Session

Do not place seeds on angels. Combining the attention response with the NPC’s programmed intervention creates a deus ex machina effect: events fall into place too conveniently. The encounter feels contrived, and the agent rejects the simulation.

The agent must choose to approach and talk to the angel without that prompt. Review their motivations and behavior with the AI so the expected circumstance offers an opportunity they are likely to engage with. A job offer or an offer of clothing may steer the agent without asking them to help anyone. The NPC remains the person they were: you cannot turn a shopkeeper into a doctor to create the encounter.

The programmed addition and its effects carry forward into later simulations. If an NPC supplies an item, it is no longer in that NPC's possession afterward. Review the existing history before adding another intervention; a later appearance does not restore the NPC to their original state.

Review the experience from the ghost perspective. Work with the AI to understand where progress stops and develop an intervention. Review what happens before deciding on another action.

The AI continues routine work between requests for your involvement. An operator can therefore assist several agents without attending continuously to every session. Refresh after agent training sessions as covered in your maintenance instructions.

For setting-specific preparation, read Reading a Historical World. The archivist can provide dated local references.

Operator Journal

Keep three journal entries each day: morning, midday, and evening. Record your observations and responses to the work. Additional entries may be added when needed.

Today's Exercise

Open the constructed training example provided in the demonstration. Locate its level goal, review the supplied ghost, and find the AI's request for assistance. Become familiar with where an intervention would be prepared and where its outcome would be reviewed.

This example is an exercise, not an assigned person. Today is for finding your way around the console. Guided intervention practice and readiness exercises follow on Day 003. Actual assignments begin on Day 004.

For further guidance on your responsibilities, see advisor from previous cohort.

records.title: What Is A-HAVA?
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation

Release: Mission Day 002, after the operator-console introduction

A-HAVA stands for Ascending Harness Activated Vessel Agent. It prepares people to coexist with other human essences inside the Artifact. The A-HAVA Institute is the institution where that training takes place.

The system builds on HAVA, the technology that lets a person experience a simulated world while their body remains in a pod. Evelyn Burroughs developed A-HAVA for ascension training. The campus pods support that training; integration into the Artifact takes place separately aboard the ship.

Learning Through Experience

An agent is the person undertaking training. Their vessel is the simulated character they inhabit. Across worlds and levels, agents encounter situations in which their responses matter. A level has a defined goal; progress depends on the agent's response, not simply on time spent in the simulation.

The AI manages routine training and adapts circumstances to the person. Human operators assist when the AI cannot produce further progress. You may help several agents because most sessions proceed without your continuous involvement. Your work is conducted through the console and recorded experiences, without meeting the agents physically.

Reviewing and Intervening

A ghost is a fixed record of an agent's session. Reviewing it helps you understand what they noticed, what they chose, and where progress stopped. Reviewing a ghost does not alter that recorded history.

A seed is placed on an object or person to draw the agent's attention through a brief sixth-sense response. It does not decide what they do next.

An angel is an NPC programmed with a function that nudges the agent in a direction. An offer of a job or clothing may serve that purpose, provided it fits the NPC's established character and role. The addition and its consequences persist into future simulations: an item supplied is no longer with the NPC. A seed cannot be placed on an angel.

Today's console example introduces the work. Tomorrow's practice covers the tools and procedures in detail. No real agents are assigned during orientation.

Your Own Condition

Refresh sessions assess Maat and Chaos while you work outside the Artifact. Follow the care guidance and your measured results. A refresh is distinct from a training session or ghost review.

See advisor from previous cohort for further guidance.

Together, we ascend.

records.title: Reading a Historical World
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation Release: Mission Day 002, after the console demonstration

Start with the scene's date and location. The worlds run through changing societies; a world name alone does not tell you which government, technologies, or customs apply.

Observe who knows whom, who can make an offer, and who is free to refuse it. Clothing, language, and forms of address can provide clues, but do not establish a person's motives or authority by themselves. Appearance does not reliably identify nationality, religion, or allegiance.

A seed draws attention. Choose its host with an understanding of what the person or object means in this scene. Attention does not guarantee agreement or action.

An angel remains the existing NPC. A shopkeeper may have goods to offer; that does not make them a doctor, employer, or official. Check the person's circumstances and what remains in their possession before programming an opportunity. Earlier additions and their consequences persist. Never place a seed on an angel.

Ask the archivist for historical context when needed. Ordinary reference material explains the setting; it does not reveal an agent's private history or prescribe the choice they will make.

records.title: Questions from Your Cohort
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Archivist / Orientation
Release: Mission Day 003, breakfast

The following subjects have occurred frequently in questions received during your first two days on campus. This reference brings the answers together for your cohort.

What is the Mission?

The Mission is to complete humanity’s collective ascension. The remaining humans must complete their training, enter the ship’s pods, and integrate into the Artifact. The fully populated Artifact is then returned to the podium on the Bridge.

What are we helping people do?

A-HAVA prepares people to coexist safely with other human essences inside the Artifact. The AI manages their training. Operators help when its interventions are no longer sufficient to produce progress.

How many people remain?

About 300 people remain to complete ascension training. Your cohort is responsible for helping them progress. Individual assignments begin on Mission Day 004.

Why were we awakened last?

Your cohort was reserved for the most difficult remaining cases because its members had the highest potential operator scores. The order of cohorts reflects that selection; being awakened last does not mean being least suited to the work.

Potential describes an expected capacity. You will still learn the console, work with the AI, review outcomes, and maintain your own condition.

What is a cohort?

A group of operators awakened to carry out the Mission. Your cohort has twenty-four members, designated A through X in awakening order. X is the final operator of this cohort.

Who is our advisor?

The advisor is the last operator of the preceding cohort. The usual handoff includes an opening briefing and brief conversations with incoming operators about their duties and campus life.

For further guidance on your cohort’s handoff, see advisor from previous cohort.

What do Maat and Chaos tell us?

They measure aspects of your condition relevant to returning to the Artifact. Maat describes order, harmony, and balance; Chaos describes disorder and imbalance. A refresh assesses these through an AI-guided A-HAVA session.

Feelings and questions are normal. They are not, on their own, a yellow or red result. Follow your measured result and the refresh procedure.

How long can we remain outside?

Most operators can remain outside for approximately ninety days. Individual limits vary. Refreshes guide your daily routine and any need for recovery or return; the typical duration does not replace those assessments.

Where can we find further answers?

Ask the archivist about the Mission, campus operations, the Great Fall, pre-Fall life, and prominent A-HAVA figures. Use the released orientation references for routine procedures and keep your own observations in your journal.

records.title: Practice and Readiness
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 003, breakfast

Today’s exercises use constructed scenarios and supplied session records. They are not real assignments and do not contribute to anyone’s ascension. Actual agent work begins tomorrow.

Morning: An Intervention

Open the practice session at your console. The AI will ask for help when the agent is not progressing toward its goal. Review the supplied ghost and practice using angels and seeds to help it achieve that goal.

Choose your intervention, review the response, and adjust as needed. Record what you tried and what happened.

Afternoon: Several Cases

Use the supplied training examples to practice moving between requests for assistance. One example is ready for review, another awaits an intervention, and another is continuing under AI management.

Identify which needs your involvement. Review or prepare the relevant intervention, then return attention to the other cases when needed. You are not expected to observe every moment of every session.

Follow the scheduled refresh and meal breaks between practice blocks.

Individual Readiness Exercise

Complete a constructed request for assistance using the console and AI guidance:

  1. Locate the goal and the point where progress stopped.
  2. Review the supplied ghost.
  3. Prepare an intervention with the AI.
  4. Review its demonstrated outcome.
  5. Record what happened and identify whether further work or a handoff would be appropriate.

The exercise checks that you can follow the process with the available assistance. Ask for clarification when a step is unclear. Readiness does not require memorizing every world or level.

For further guidance on beginning operator work, see advisor from previous cohort.

records.title: Japan — Everyday Life and Social Expectations
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation Release: Mission Day 003, morning practice

Period Bearings

The Meiji period runs from 1868 to 1912. Later scenes belong to different periods; do not carry one scene's assumptions unchanged toward World War II. The state, its institutions, and Japan's imperial reach changed during this span.

What to Notice

Kimono and Western clothing could coexist during Meiji. Dress varied with occupation, circumstances, and the wearer. A change of clothing does not necessarily indicate a change of date.

Check household and workplace relationships before interpreting deference, silence, or an invitation. Do not assume one gesture has the same meaning for every person. Identify who owns an object and who has permission to offer it.

Japan’s first railway opened in 1872, between Shimbashi and Yokohama. Railways and newer communications belong to a changing infrastructure, not a uniform level of access. Check the particular town and year before adding a journey, message, or manufactured item. An available technology is not necessarily available to this NPC.

Before Intervening

Review the scene's supplies and relationships. The agent still has to choose the encounter; a historically plausible offer is not a guaranteed result.

For a particular custom, institution, or conflict, request a dated local reference from the archivist. This sheet is an introduction, not a complete history.

records.title: Sessions and Handoffs
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation
Release: Mission Day 003, after the morning handoff briefing

Session Timing

The pod collects neural activity, biofeedback, and other vital readings. The AI reviews these alongside the agent's behavior during each session.

Successful sessions can be short: a person progressing quickly may complete a session in fifteen to twenty minutes. Failed sessions can take several hours.

A completed session is not necessarily a completed level, and completing one level is not the same as completing a world or the entire training.

Assignment Readiness

The AI selects requests according to operator readiness as well as an agent's need. Some agents wait for suitable operator assistance. Assignments centered on more intense situations are normally deferred until you have spent several weeks outside.

An otherwise manageable setting may contain an unexpected distressing encounter. Report it and follow refresh guidance; assignment screening is not a guarantee about everything you might see.

Operator Attempts

Each operator has up to ten attempts at a level before the agent is handed off. Work with the AI, review the ghost and the result, and keep an account of the interventions you have tried.

If you cannot continue before that allowance is used, request a handoff. A handoff changes the operator responsible for assisting; it does not by itself indicate that the agent completed the level.

Your Account of the Work

Record the relevant goal, your intervention, what happened, and questions that remain. Keep observations separate from explanations you have not established. Individual agent details belong in your journal.

You do not have direct access to other operators’ personal journals. This orientation reference contains procedures, not individual case histories.

Starting Tomorrow

Consult your work schedule and open your console for the first assignments on Mission Day 004. The AI continues routine training and requests your involvement when progress is stalled. Several agents may be progressing while you attend to one request.

Refresh after agent training sessions and before bed, or whenever you feel a need. Follow the yellow recovery process if that is your result.

records.title: Germany — Everyday Life and Changing Authority
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation Release: Mission Day 003, after afternoon practice

Period Bearings

The German Empire ended in 1918. The Weimar Republic followed; Nazi rule began in 1933 and ended in 1945. World War I and World War II must not be treated as one continuous conflict. Check which institutions hold power at the scene's date.

What to Notice

A city street can include shops, rail travel, and printed notices. The availability of goods and money changes with the year. In particular, do not reuse prices across the inflation of 1923.

Clothing and forms of address may suggest occupation or expectations, but do not establish someone's beliefs. Ask what a person can actually do within their household, workplace, and legal circumstances.

Check the year and setting before assuming access to a telephone, radio, or private transport. A railway connection does not mean everyone has equal freedom to travel.

Before Intervening

An offer must fit the NPC's resources and position. Historical restrictions can change what is possible even when the same shop or person appears again. Consult the archivist rather than inventing an exception.

records.title: Hawaii — Community and Everyday Life
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Orientation Release: Mission Day 003, final preparation

Period Bearings

Hawaii's monarchy was overthrown in 1893. U.S. annexation followed in 1898 and territorial government in 1900. These changes were contested; do not describe all residents as sharing one view. The islands were not a U.S. state during the training period.

What to Notice

Native Hawaiian identity is distinct from simply residing in Hawaii. Communities include people with different languages, ancestries, occupations, and family histories. A person's appearance does not tell you their citizenship, loyalties, or preferred language.

Plantation work, town life, and tourism place people in different circumstances. Check local transport and the person's resources before arranging an opportunity; do not assume movement between islands is immediate.

Music is part of the setting, not merely background. Hawaiian traditions include chant as well as changing song and instrumental practices. Steel guitar is one sound you may encounter in twentieth-century scenes; it does not represent every musical tradition in the islands.

Before Intervening

Identify the actual relationship between an NPC and the agent before creating an invitation or offer. Do not substitute a general idea of hospitality for that person's established character.

Daily life changed significantly across this period. Consult a reference for the scene's date rather than assuming a familiar place still works the same way.

records.title: The Fall and the Loss of Connection
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Archive / Historical Reference
Compiled by: Archivist
Available: Mission Day 007

The Great Fall began with the arrival of the ship on June 6, 2076, forty-nine years after the first arcology launched in 2027 and approximately one thousand years ago. Its arrival produced interference with wireless systems. The term names that initiating event as well as, in common use, the collapse associated with it.

Pre-Fall devices depended heavily on remote services collectively called the cloud. Instructions and information were available through those connections rather than held entirely within each device. Even routine machines could stop functioning when the connection failed.

Physical equipment did not have to be destroyed to become unusable. The interruption separated working components from the systems they depended on. Civilization's reliance on those connections made the consequences immediate and widespread.

What Continued to Work

Wired technology remained usable. Surviving equipment could be connected directly and repurposed, although the survival of a component did not preserve the larger society around it.

Present-day wireless task robots carry limited instructions and knowledge for their assigned work. Robots requiring active data use wired connections. Some robots work untethered between visits to a base station, where they connect physically to transfer collected data and receive new instructions. These are different operating requirements, not a division between functioning and nonfunctioning robots.

The continuing operation of wired infrastructure made salvage and later reconstruction possible.

records.title: Life in the Monolithic Cities
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Archive / Historical Reference
Compiled by: Archivist
Available: Mission Day 007

The Monolithic Cities were enormous ocean arcologies where most pre-Fall humans lived. Much of daily experience took place through HAVA while physical bodies remained in pods. AI systems operated the virtual worlds, and robots maintained much of the physical infrastructure.

Global One Network was the corporation that owned the cities and HAVA. The first test arcology launched off Oman in 2027 and housed one million people. Demand surged within a few years; rapid expansion brought most of the population into the ocean cities and their pods before the Fall.

A person in a HAVA world was its agent. The character they inhabited was their vessel. Those terms describe a person's relationship to the system, not the purpose of the particular world.

HAVA existed before ascension training. The human-built pods used on campus descend from that technology. They are distinct from the white ship pods associated with the Artifact.

Surviving Material

The destruction of the cities did not erase every component or record. Surviving HAVA pods and usable equipment were recovered and transported to the ship in Colorado. Wired connections allowed salvaged components to be used in later systems.

Recovered material can document aspects of city life without providing a complete account of every resident's fate. This reference does not supply a pre-Fall population total or a verified death toll.

records.title: Bring Purpose Back — Advertisement
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Archive / Pre-Fall Advertising Collection
Format: Recruitment advertisement
Available: Mission Day 007, after Entry 1

Advertisement Text

BRING PURPOSE BACK

A place to live. A reason to begin.

Discover arcology living.

Image Description

A waterfront residence curves around sheltered water, its terraces lined with greenery. Beside it, two people work together at a wooden bench. The advertisement presents both beneath the promise to bring purpose back.

Archive note: The advertiser, location, and exact date are not established by the surviving copy.

records.title: Berlin — Deportation by Rail
records.html:
Source: A-HAVA Archive / Historical Reference Available: Mission Day 007, after Entry 1 Context: Follow-up to the Germany-world scene reviewed on Mission Day 006

The scene is set near Berlin-Moabit freight station in 1943. Transports represented in this simulation were bound for Auschwitz in German-occupied Poland.

Auschwitz was a concentration camp complex. Being sent there was not an ordinary journey or a lawful consequence of wrongdoing by the people deported. Nazi racial persecution targeted people the regime classified as Jewish.

This occurred during World War II but cannot be explained simply as fighting between armies. Civilian institutions, including the railways, participated in deportation.

The simulation's individual people and conversation are constructed. They are not a recovered record of a named victim's final journey. A ghost preserves what occurred in that simulation; it does not replace historical evidence.

Further references on related topics will be available after Week 3.
